lost-myself.name: Lost myself
lost-myself.line: I've spent so long looking after everyone else that I don't know what I want any more.
lost-myself.why: Keeps the loss of self but shows what it looks like day to day: a life spent on other people's needs, and no answer when someone asks what you want. The name also matches the ID again.

lost-myself.name: Who I am
lost-myself.line: I can't say what I like, what I want or who I am any more.
lost-myself.why: Stays close to the original and to people who lost themselves after a big change, not only through caregiving, while giving concrete things a person notices they can't answer.

procrastination.name: Follow-through
procrastination.line: I keep putting off the things that matter to me until it's too late.
procrastination.why: An area-style name so the Purpose heading doesn't mix problem and area labels, and a line that says what the putting off costs instead of only naming the habit.

stuck.name: Progress
stuck.line: I feel like my life isn't going anywhere, and each year looks like the last.
stuck.why: An area-style name so the heading reads one way, and a line that adds something to picture: years that look the same.

pairs.distinction: Learning is wanting to learn something for myself and not knowing how to begin; Skills is the world or my job now asking for skills I don't have.
pairs.reason: Wanting to pick up guitar and falling behind at work feel nothing alike, so a person knows which one is theirs.

pairs.distinction: Learning is about starting on a subject or skill; Direction is about a bigger goal in life and the steps to reach it.
pairs.reason: Someone who wants to learn Spanish and someone who wants a different life would each pick their own line without hesitating.

pairs.distinction: Direction is not knowing the steps toward a goal; Skills is knowing what's needed and not being able to do it yet.
pairs.reason: Missing a map and missing the ability are different gaps, and the fixes for each are different.

pairs.distinction: Stuck is feeling that life isn't moving at all, often without a clear goal; Direction is having a goal and no route to it.
pairs.reason: The line for Direction starts with knowing what I want, which someone who feels stuck usually can't say, so the choice is easy.

pairs.distinction: Lost myself is not knowing what I like or want any more; Stuck is knowing my life isn't moving forward.
pairs.reason: One is about who I am and the other is about where my life is going, and the alternative line for Lost myself makes that plain.

pairs.distinction: Lost myself is not knowing myself any more; Self-esteem is judging myself harshly.
pairs.reason: Someone who has lost track of what they want isn't necessarily hard on themselves, and the reverse is true too.

pairs.distinction: Procrastination is not starting the things I mean to do; Focus is my mind wandering once I've started.
pairs.reason: People can tell putting something off from drifting away from it partway through.

pairs.distinction: Career is being in the wrong line of work; Direction is knowing what I want, in work or anywhere else, and not how to get there.
pairs.reason: Someone in the wrong job may not yet know what they want instead, while Direction starts from a goal already in mind.

pairs.distinction: Career is about the job; Stuck is about life as a whole not moving.
pairs.reason: A person who likes their work can still feel their life is going nowhere, so the two don't collapse into one.

pairs.distinction: Creativity is missing making things; Fun is missing play and lightness of any kind.
pairs.reason: Someone who misses painting and someone who never gets to relax and play would each recognize only their own line.

pairs.distinction: Creativity is no longer making things of my own; Meaning is feeling my paid work doesn't matter.
pairs.reason: One is about time to create and the other is about whether a job is worth doing, and people know which they mean.

meaning-in-life.name: Meaning in life
meaning-in-life.line: I don't know what my life is for.

sources.passage: Nearly 3 in 5 young adults (58%) reported that they lacked “meaning or purpose” in their lives in the previous month.
Almost 1 in 10 adults (9%) reported low levels of feeling that the things they do in life are worthwhile; this was more common among adults aged 16 to 29 years (14%) and 30 to 49 years (11%).

meaning-in-life.prevalence: 58% of U.S. young adults said they lacked meaning or purpose in the previous month (Harvard Making Caring Common). In Great Britain, 9% of adults report low levels of feeling that what they do is worthwhile, 14% among those aged 16 to 29 (ONS).

dont-know-what-i-want.name: What I want
dont-know-what-i-want.line: I don't know what I want to do with my life.
aliases: Not knowing what to do with my life

sources.passage: Half of young adults reported that their mental health was negatively influenced by “not knowing what to do with my life.”

dont-know-what-i-want.prevalence: Half of U.S. young adults said "not knowing what to do with my life" hurt their mental health (Harvard Making Caring Common).

reading.name: Reading
reading.line: Reading forms, letters and instructions is hard for me.

sources.passage: Between 2017 and 2023, there were increases in the percentages of adults performing at the lowest proficiency level (Level 1 or below) in both literacy and numeracy: in literacy this percentage increased from 19 to 28 percent and in numeracy from 29 to 34 percent.
The average rate of literacy needs across the OECD is 26%

reading.prevalence: 28 percent of U.S. adults read at Level 1 or below, up from 19 percent in 2017 (NCES, PIAAC 2023). The OECD average is 26%.

everyday-math.name: Math
everyday-math.line: Everyday math, like working out a bill or a discount, is hard for me.

sources.passage: Between 2017 and 2023, there were increases in the percentages of adults performing at the lowest proficiency level (Level 1 or below) in both literacy and numeracy: in literacy this percentage increased from 19 to 28 percent and in numeracy from 29 to 34 percent.
The average rate of numeracy needs across the OECD is 25%.

everyday-math.prevalence: 34 percent of U.S. adults are at Level 1 or below in numeracy, up from 29 percent in 2017 (NCES, PIAAC 2023). The OECD average is 25%.

computers.name: Computers
computers.line: I struggle to do things on a computer or phone that everyone now expects.

sources.passage: About 16 percent of U.S. adults are not digitally literate, compared to 23 percent of adults internationally.

computers.prevalence: About 16 percent of U.S. adults are not digitally literate, compared to 23 percent internationally (NCES/AIR, PIAAC).

english.name: English
english.line: I don't speak English well enough to get by.

sources.passage: Over three-quarters (78.3%) of the nation age 5 and older spoke only English at home, according to newly released 2018-2022 American Community Survey (ACS), 5-year estimates.

Among the population age 5 and older that spoke a language other than English at home, 61.0% of Spanish speakers, 48.2% of Chinese speakers (which includes all dialects), and 69.8% of Tagalog (including Filipino) speakers spoke English “very well.”

english.prevalence: In 2018-2022, 78.3% of U.S. residents age 5 and older spoke only English at home. Among those who spoke another language, 61.0% of Spanish speakers and 48.2% of Chinese speakers spoke English "very well" (Census ACS).

diploma.name: Diploma
diploma.line: I never finished high school, and it holds me back.

sources.passage: In 2022, the highest level of education of the population age 25 and older in the United States ranged from less than high school to advanced degrees beyond a bachelor’s degree. 9% had less than a high school diploma or equivalent.

diploma.prevalence: In 2022, 9% of U.S. adults age 25 and older had less than a high school diploma or equivalent (Census Bureau).

no-time-to-learn.name: Classes
no-time-to-learn.line: I want to take a class or training, but I can't fit it around work, family or money.

sources.passage: Of those who wanted to participate and could not (10.2%) or those who participated but wanted to participate more (15.7%), 25.3% listed training schedules as the main barrier to their participation, while 16.0% cited family reasons, and 15.2% highlighted costs

no-time-to-learn.prevalence: Among EU adults who wanted more education or training, 25.3% named schedules as the main barrier, 16.0% family reasons and 15.2% costs (European Commission employment and social developments report).

data.notes: Sixteen lists read. oecd.org returned 403, so OECD entries are the framework's Knowledge and skills and Subjective well-being dimensions as named in docs/spec/pains/pain-inventory.md, with Survey of Adult Skills 2023 averages taken from NALA's factsheet and the NEET passage from TUAC's summary of How's Life 2024. The 211 2025 Impact Snapshot and WHO/IHME cause-of-burden lists were checked; no category bears on Purpose, so they are not recorded as lists. Pew's 'Where Americans find meaning in life' (2018) was read but lists sources of meaning, not pains, so it is not a list here. Wikidata QIDs came from about 10 wbsearchentities lookups before the API rate-limited this session; no QID was found for limited English proficiency, NEET or dropping out. Overlaps for refine: meaning-in-life with meaningless-work (Meaning, work only) and stuck; dont-know-what-i-want with no-path (which assumes the person knows what they want); no-time-to-learn with learning; reading, everyday-math and computers sit under need-skills; english may also belong to People or Home for new arrivals. Harvard's figures are for U.S. young adults (18-25), not all adults; ESDE figures are EU adults who wanted more training.

proposed.name: English
proposed.line: I don't speak English well enough to get by.

why.detail: In 2018-2022, 78.3% of U.S. residents age 5 and older spoke only English at home. Among those who spoke another language, 61.0% of Spanish speakers and 48.2% of Chinese speakers spoke English "very well" (Census ACS).

sources.passage: Over three-quarters (78.3%) of the nation age 5 and older spoke only English at home, according to newly released 2018-2022 American Community Survey (ACS), 5-year estimates.

Among the population age 5 and older that spoke a language other than English at home, 61.0% of Spanish speakers, 48.2% of Chinese speakers (which includes all dialects), and 69.8% of Tagalog (including Filipino) speakers spoke English “very well.”
